headline: Three Investigations on Chinese Platforms, and What They Don't Prove
context: WeChat and RedNote operate under PRC content rules. Malaysia licensed WeChat and TikTok in Jan 2025 but the Online Safety Act 2025 excludes private messaging. A Merdeka/UM survey found Chinese-Malaysian favourability of China rose from 41% to 67% (2016 to 2022).

changes.summary: Correction: Earlier editions included a 2016 to 2022 Malay favourability figure and a claim about Malay-language TikTok disinformation that the sources did not support as stated; both are removed.

Correction: we no longer say TikTok runs under Chinese content rules or that no rule requires platforms to disclose their moderation algorithms; our sources show only that the Online Safety Act sets no express duty to do so.

cards.big: Three different investigations point at three different things about Chinese-owned platforms; bundling them produces a story stronger than the evidence.
cards.sub: Citizen Lab, Sinopsis and ISEAS document three separate findings, not one. The shared thread is opacity, not what readers believe.

cards.big: WeChat surveils images and documents shared between non-China accounts to train its China-side censorship system
cards.sub: Citizen Lab documented this in 2020. The same paper is explicit it could not test chat-text between non-China accounts and found no evidence linking it to CCP direction.

cards.big: Malaysia licensed WeChat and TikTok in Jan 2025, but the Online Safety Act 2025 excludes private messaging from its scope
cards.sub: Licences regulate presence. The Act regulates harmful content but not private messages, and sets no express duty to disclose moderation algorithms to MCMC.

cards.big: Chinese-Malaysian favourability of China rose from 41% to 67% between 2016 and 2022, a Merdeka Center/UM survey found
cards.sub: RFA and Oriental Daily reported the joint survey. It measured favourable views of China, not belief in any specific narrative.

cards.big: The question is not which Malaysian community believes Beijing. It is whether any user (Chinese, Malay, Tamil, English) sees how their platform decides what news reaches them.
Think of it like a landlord who decides which tenants' mail gets delivered
cards.sub: The landlord writes the rules, the rules are not public, and Malaysia's Online Safety Act does not expressly require the landlord to show them. WeChat, TikTok, RedNote, Facebook, Telegram are all landlords.

cards.big: PRC platforms carry a legal duty US and EU platforms do not. Malaysia regulates platform presence more than moderation logic
cards.sub: Name the asymmetry (PRC National Intelligence Law Art 7), then apply the same transparency rules to every platform, in every language.
